context: The author's earlier papers replace the semigroup by a \emph{hemigroup}: a family of operators $\Phi_{s,t}$ from scale $s$ to scale $t$ in which two consecutive steps compose to one, $\Phi_{t,u}\Phi_{s,t} = \Phi_{s,u}$. This cascade ties the scale to no additive parameter. With continuity in scale, symmetry, positivity and covariance under every dilation, the hemigroup axioms classify the families of kernels on the line \prog{V-line v0.1}{Thm.~7.3, p.~37}, and in $\RR^d$ the isotropic ones \prog{iso v0.1}{Thm.~3.6, p.~13}. Covariance under every dilation is more than a pyramid needs, since a pyramid is looked at only at the scales $q^n$. This paper keeps the cascade, continuity, positivity and nondegeneracy, requires symmetry or rotation invariance where a result needs it, and requires covariance at the one ratio $q$ only.

This paper rests on five releases of the author's earlier work, cited at the printed number and page. The line paper \progpaper{V-line v0.1} states the axioms on the line and classifies the families that satisfy them. Two companion papers were released with it. The first, its \emph{cone module} \progpaper{V-cone v0.1}, describes these families as a convex cone, with their generators and their computation on the line. The second, its \emph{selection module} \progpaper{V-selection v0.1}, treats locality and the non-creation of extrema. The isotropic paper \progpaper{iso v0.1} carries the axioms and the classification to $\RR^d$. The affine paper \progpaper{affine v0.1} supplies the frame families, which the supplement uses for the separability of the classical kernels.

A law is \emph{self-decomposable} if, for every $0 < c < 1$, it is the law of $cX + Y$ with $X$ of that law and $Y$ independent of $X$ [\sscite{sato1999levy}, Def.~15.1, p.~90] (Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable}). Shrinking the law by any factor and adding independent noise gives it back. These laws are the kernels of scale-space theory. On the line the kernels of the fully covariant families are exactly the symmetric self-decomposable laws \prog{V-line v0.1}{Thm.~7.3, p.~37}. In $\RR^d$, with rotation invariance, they are exactly the rotation-invariant self-decomposable laws \prog{iso v0.1}{Thm.~3.6, p.~13}, whose exponents are the $F(|\cdot|)$ with $F \in \mathcal{A}_d$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:cited-A35}(2)).

The isotropic paper reduces an isotropic family to its marginal along one line through the origin. The marginal is the image of each kernel under $x \mapsto \langle e, x\rangle$ for a unit vector $e$, the projection of tomography \prog{iso v0.1}{\S~3.2, p.~12}. The argument has two halves. The marginals form a family on the line with the same covariance, and the classification on the line then gives their transforms. Under one dilation the first half survives. The second does not, because a family on the line need not be a marginal.

The classification fails. \prog{iso v0.1}{Thm.~3.6, p.~13} applies the line's theorem to the marginals, and that theorem assumes (A8) for every $\lambda$. Under one dilation Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-strata} takes its place. The line's examples of the lower strata do not lift either. They are built from atoms in the \Levy{} measure, and in $d \ge 2$ the \Levy{} measure of a marginal has none.

The fully covariant classes are nested, $\mathcal{A}_{d+1} \subseteq \mathcal{A}_d$ \prog{iso v0.1}{Prop.~2.6, p.~8}, and the inclusion is strict in every dimension \prog{iso v0.1}{Prop.~3.22(2), p.~27}. The next proposition is the counterpart under one dilation. For a pyramid it means that a radial exponent that serves one ratio in the plane need not serve it in $\RR^3$. Its witness has a \Levy{} measure carried by spheres, where the isotropic paper's has a profile with a jump.

Conditions (a)--(c) are what the axioms of \prog{iso v0.1}{Def.~3.2, p.~11} say about the laws of the operators $\Phi_{s,t}$, with two changes. The strata place the pyramids among the families of scale space. The dilations under which a symmetric family is covariant form $\{1\}$, some $q^{\ZZ}$, or all of $(0,\infty)$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:family-dilations}(2)). So covariance under the powers of one ratio is the only case between none and every dilation. For isotropic families each stratum is strictly larger than the next (Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice-strata-strict}). The pyramids of stratum~2 therefore form a wider class than the fully covariant families that the isotropic paper classifies \prog{iso v0.1}{Thm.~3.6, p.~13}. Lindeberg's scale space for discrete signals \cite{lindeberg1990scalespace} lies in stratum~1 and not in stratum~2 (Proposition~\ref{prop:lindeberg-stratum-one} of the supplement). It is no pyramid in this sense.
